meta_title: Integrate e^(-3x) cos^3 x dx — NCERT Exemplar Q42
meta_desc: Solve NCERT Exemplar Class 12 Q42, the integral of e^(-3x) cos^3 x dx, using cos^3 x expansion and the e^(ax) cos(bx) formula, with a free 8-question quiz.

quiz.title: Integrating e^(ax) cos(bx) Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on integrating exponential times cosine, the power-reduction of cos^3 x, and putting the pieces together. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Exemplar Class 12 integration — e^(-3x) cos^3 x

questions.q: Which identity turns cos^3 x into a sum of single cosines?
questions.explanation: From cos 3x = 4 cos^3 x - 3 cos x, solving for cos^3 x gives cos^3 x = (3 cos x + cos 3x)/4. This linearises the cube so each term is a standard e^(ax) cos(bx) integral.

questions.q: What is the standard result for ∫ e^(ax) cos(bx) dx?
options: e^(ax)(a sin bx - b cos bx)/(a^2 + b^2) + C
e^(ax)(a cos bx + b sin bx)/(a^2 + b^2) + C
e^(ax)(cos bx + sin bx)/(a + b) + C
e^(ax)(a cos bx - b sin bx)/(a^2 - b^2) + C
questions.explanation: The classic formula is ∫ e^(ax) cos(bx) dx = e^(ax)(a cos bx + b sin bx)/(a^2 + b^2) + C, derived by integration by parts twice.

questions.q: For this problem, e^(-3x) cos^3 x, what value of a appears in every exponential integral?
questions.explanation: The common factor is e^(-3x), so a = -3 throughout. Only the cosine frequency b changes between the two terms (b = 1 and b = 3).

questions.q: After expanding, which two integrals must you evaluate?
options: ∫ e^(-3x) sin x dx and ∫ e^(-3x) sin 3x dx
∫ e^(-3x) cos x dx and ∫ e^(-3x) sin 3x dx
∫ e^(3x) cos x dx and ∫ e^(3x) cos 3x dx
∫ e^(-3x) cos x dx and ∫ e^(-3x) cos 3x dx
questions.explanation: cos^3 x = (3 cos x + cos 3x)/4, so e^(-3x) cos^3 x = (3/4) e^(-3x) cos x + (1/4) e^(-3x) cos 3x. Both remaining pieces are e^(ax) cos(bx) integrals.

options: e^(-3x)(-3 cos x + sin x)/10 + C
e^(-3x)(3 cos x + sin x)/10 + C
e^(-3x)(-3 cos x - sin x)/9 + C
questions.explanation: Here a = -3, b = 1, so a^2 + b^2 = 10 and the result is e^(-3x)(-3 cos x + 1·sin x)/10 + C = e^(-3x)(sin x - 3 cos x)/10 + C.
With a = -3, b = 3, a^2 + b^2 = 9 + 9 = 18, giving e^(-3x)(-3 cos 3x + 3 sin 3x)/18 + C, which simplifies to e^(-3x)(sin 3x - cos 3x)/6 + C.

questions.q: Combining the two results, ∫ e^(-3x) cos^3 x dx equals which expression (before simplifying)?
questions.explanation: Multiply each integral by its coefficient from the expansion: 3/4 times the cos x result plus 1/4 times the cos 3x result. Then add a single constant C.

questions.q: Why do you write only one constant of integration for the whole answer?
options: Definite integrals never need a constant
Because cos^3 x is an odd function
The sum of two arbitrary constants is itself a single arbitrary constant
questions.explanation: Each integral contributes an arbitrary constant, but any sum of constants is still an arbitrary constant, so one C at the end covers the whole indefinite integral.

faq.q: Why expand cos^3 x instead of integrating it directly?
faq.a: There is no simple product rule for e^(-3x) times cos^3 x as it stands. Writing cos^3 x = (3 cos x + cos 3x)/4 turns the cube into single cosines, so every term becomes a standard e^(ax) cos(bx) integral you already know how to solve.

faq.q: Where does the identity cos^3 x = (3 cos x + cos 3x)/4 come from?
faq.a: It comes from the triple-angle formula cos 3x = 4 cos^3 x - 3 cos x. Rearranging for cos^3 x gives 4 cos^3 x = cos 3x + 3 cos x, so cos^3 x = (3 cos x + cos 3x)/4.

faq.q: How is the formula for ∫ e^(ax) cos(bx) dx derived?
faq.a: Apply integration by parts twice; the original integral reappears, and you solve the resulting equation for it. The result is e^(ax)(a cos bx + b sin bx)/(a^2 + b^2) + C, which you can quote directly in exams.

faq.q: Do the signs of a and b matter in the formula?
faq.a: The denominator a^2 + b^2 is always positive, so only the numerator carries the signs. With a = -3 the cosine term picks up the minus sign, which is why answers show terms like (sin x - 3 cos x).
